subject: Path models with three endogenous variables: How to interpret the estimates and compare models?

messages.author: 8fd20a508c70a9d2
messages.subject: Path models with three endogenous variables: How to interpret the estimates and compare models?
parts:
Hi,

I have two models; model6_1 and model7_1. Pictures and code with results below.

Both models have three endogeneous (dependent) variables; own_social_factors1, lapsi_mttke0615_2 and own_health_factors_0105_2/lapsi_mtsompoliosasto1_0105 (depending the model and is the only differ between the models)
and one exogenous (independent) variable. All variables are binary. 

1) How can I compare those two models, because in binary situation, lavaan doesn't print any AIC or BIC statistics.
Is it correct to compare chisq-values, and say the smaller chisq value the better model (model 6_1: 823.823 vs model7_1:545.740). In this example, model7_1 would be better, right?

2a) How can I interpret estimates?
Let's say estimate for parental_mental_health_8700_2 is 0.164. Is it correct to say that when value of parental_mental_health_8700_2 changes from 0 to 1, z-score rise 0.164?

2b) Total effect is 0.232. Probability to get value 1 of variable lapsi_mtke0615_2 under model6_1 is (1dnorm(0.232,0,1)) 0.61156509?

3) What are those thresholds-values. How to interpret them?

4) Can I multiply estimates in binary case also for example under model6_1, direct effect is (a*b) + (d*e)?

Thank you for your support and answers already!

messages.subject: Re: Path models with three endogenous variables: How to interpret the estimates and compare models?
parts: 1) How can I compare those two models, because in binary situation, lavaan doesn't print any AIC or BIC statistics.
This is irrelevant in your case because both models are saturated (they have zero degrees of freedom, and therefore have arbitrarily perfect fit).
Is it correct to compare chisq-values, and say the smaller chisq value the better model (model 6_1: 823.823 vs model7_1:545.740). In this example, model7_1 would be better, right?
You are looking at the values for the baseline model (used to calculate CFI and TLI), not your hypothesized model.
2a) How can I interpret estimates?

It is probit regression:

https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/42956/how-do-i-interpret-a-probit-model-in-stata
2b) Total effect is 0.232. Probability to get value 1 of variable lapsi_mtke0615_2 under model6_1 is (1dnorm(0.232,0,1)) 0.61156509?

This depends on whether you use delta parameterization (total variance of latent response = 1) or theta parameterization (residual variance of latent response = 1).  But I think you have the right idea.
3) What are those thresholds-values. How to interpret them?
4) Can I multiply estimates in binary case also for example under model6_1, direct effect is (a*b) + (d*e)?

There are some issues that I am not familiar with, but there are some notes you might find useful in this presentation (starting with slide 22):

http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/pages/en/Presentations/Presentation%20Yves%20Rosseel.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Path models with three endogenous variables: How to interpret the estimates and compare models?
parts:
Hi,

Your model is a saturated and recursive model of observed variables. In this case it could be a lot simpler if you just estimated the model with separate logistic regressions. But the interpretation of the model and the choice of modeling strategy depends on what is your interest. Are the variables that you are interested in dichotomous (e.g. biological gender), or are they continuous but measured with dichotomous variables (e.g. a yes/no answer to a question of do you feel sick today.)? These two cases require different approaches and also the interpretation of the mediation effect would be different. 

Mikko
